{{Short description|Nonabelian group in algebraic group theory}}
[[File:Complex polygon 3-6-2.svg|thumb|The regular [[complex polytope]], 3{6}2 or {{CDD|3node_1|6|node}} or {{CDD|3node_1|3|3node_1}}, represents the [[Cayley diagram]] for the binary tetrahedral group, with each red and blue triangle a directed subgraph.<ref name="Coxeter 1975">{{cite book |last=Coxeter |first=H. S. M. |author-link=H. S. M. Coxeter |year=1975 |title=Regular Complex Polytopes |location=London, New York |publisher=Cambridge University Press |page=109 |isbn=9780521-201254 |lccn=90001999}} Fig. 11.5E</ref>]]
In [[mathematics]], the '''binary tetrahedral group''', denoted 2T or {{angbr|2,3,3}},<ref name=anglebracket>Coxeter & Moser (1980). Generators and Relations for Discrete Groups: <l,m,n>: R<sup>l</sup> = S<sup>m</sup> = T<sup>n</sup> = RST.</ref> is a certain [[nonabelian group]] of [[order (group theory)|order]] 24. It is an [[group extension|extension]] of the [[tetrahedral group]] T or (2,3,3) of order&nbsp;12 by a [[cyclic group]] of order&nbsp;2, and is the [[preimage]] of the tetrahedral group under the 2:1 [[covering homomorphism]] Spin(3)&nbsp;→&nbsp;SO(3) of the [[special orthogonal group]] by the [[spin group]]. It follows that the binary tetrahedral group is a [[discrete subgroup]] of Spin(3) of order&nbsp;24. The [[complex reflection group]] named 3(24)3 by [[Geoffrey Colin Shephard|G.C. Shephard]] or 3[3]3 and {{CDD|3node|3|3node}} by [[Coxeter]], is isomorphic to the binary tetrahedral group.

The binary tetrahedral group is most easily described concretely as a discrete subgroup of the [[unit quaternion]]s, under the isomorphism {{nowrap|Spin(3) ≅ Sp(1)}}, where [[Sp(1)]] is the multiplicative group of unit quaternions. (For a description of this homomorphism see the article on [[quaternions and spatial rotation]]s.)

==Elements==
[[File:Cayley_graph_of_SL(2,3).svg|thumb|left|160px|[[Cayley graph]] of SL(2,3)]]
{| class=wikitable align=right width=320
|+ Symmetry projections
|- align=center
|[[File:Binary tetrahedral group elements.png|160px]]<BR>8-fold <small>''Erratum''</small>{{efn|The "presentation" <math>\langle r,s,t \mid r^2 = s^3 = t^3 = -1 \rangle</math> should read <math>\langle r,s,t \mid r^2 = s^3 = t^3 = rst \rangle</math>. Any presentation is an abstract definition of a group and cannot contain −1, which is a number. Besides the relation <math>r = st</math> would be lost.}}
|[[File:Binary tetrahedral group elements 12-fold.svg|160px]]<BR>12-fold
|-
|colspan=2|
24 quaternion elements:
* 1 order-1: 1
* 1 order-2: −1
* 6 order-4: ±i, ±j, ±k
* 8 order-6: (+1 ± i ± j ± k)/2
* 8 order-3: (−1 ± i ± j ± k)/2.
|}
Explicitly, the binary tetrahedral group is given as the [[group of units]] in the [[ring (mathematics)|ring]] of [[Hurwitz integer]]s. There are 24 such units given by
:<math>\{\pm 1,\pm i,\pm j,\pm k,\tfrac{1}{2}(\pm 1 \pm i \pm j \pm k)\}</math>
with all possible sign combinations.

All 24 units have absolute value 1 and therefore lie in the unit quaternion group Sp(1). The [[convex hull]] of these 24 elements in 4-dimensional space form a [[convex regular 4-polytope]] called the [[24-cell]].
{{clear|left}}

==Properties==
The binary tetrahedral group, denoted by 2T, fits into the [[short exact sequence]]
:<math>1\to\{\pm 1\}\to 2\mathrm{T}\to \mathrm{T} \to 1.</math>
This sequence does not [[split exact sequence|split]], meaning that 2T is ''not'' a [[semidirect product]] of {±1} by T. In fact, there is no subgroup of 2T isomorphic to T.

The binary tetrahedral group is the [[covering groups of the alternating and symmetric groups|covering group]] of the tetrahedral group. Thinking of the tetrahedral group as the [[alternating group]] on four letters, {{nowrap|T ≅ A<sub>4</sub>}}, we thus have the binary tetrahedral group as the covering group, {{nowrap|2T ≅ <math>\widehat{\mathrm{A}_4}</math>.}}

The [[center of a group|center]] of 2T is the subgroup {±1}. The [[inner automorphism group]] is isomorphic to A<sub>4</sub>, and the full [[automorphism group]] is isomorphic to S<sub>4</sub>.<ref>{{cite web|title=Special linear group:SL(2,3)|url=http://groupprops.subwiki.org/wiki/Special_linear_group:SL%282,3%29#Endomorphisms|website=groupprops}}</ref>

[[Image:Versor action on Hurwitz quaternions.svg|thumb|right|Left multiplication by −''ω'', an [[order (group theory)|order]]-6 element: look at gray, blue, purple, and orange balls and arrows that constitute 4&nbsp;[[Group action (mathematics)|orbits]] (two arrows are not depicted). ''ω'' itself is the bottommost ball: {{nowrap|1=''ω'' = (−''ω'')(−1) = (−''ω'')<sup>4</sup>}}]]
The binary tetrahedral group can be written as a [[semidirect product]]
:<math>2\mathrm{T}=\mathrm{Q}\rtimes\mathrm{C}_3</math>
where Q is the [[quaternion group]] consisting of the 8 [[Lipschitz unit]]s and C<sub>3</sub> is the [[cyclic group]] of order 3 generated by {{math|1=''ω'' = &minus;{{sfrac|1|2}}(1 + ''i'' + ''j'' + ''k'')}}. The group C<sub>3</sub> acts on the normal subgroup Q by [[conjugation (group theory)|conjugation]]. Conjugation by {{math|''ω''}} is the automorphism of Q that cyclically rotates {{mvar|i}}, {{mvar|j}}, and {{mvar|k}}.

One can show that the binary tetrahedral group is isomorphic to the [[special linear group]] SL(2,3) – the group of all {{nowrap|2 × 2}} matrices over the [[finite field]] '''F'''<sub>3</sub> with unit determinant, with this isomorphism covering the isomorphism of the [[projective special linear group]] PSL(2,3) with the alternating group A<sub>4</sub>.<!-- Is there any geometric meaning to this isomorphism? -->

===Presentation===
The group 2T has a [[group presentation|presentation]] given by
:<math>\langle r,s,t \mid r^2 = s^3 = t^3 = rst \rangle</math>
or equivalently,
:<math>\langle s,t \mid (st)^2 = s^3 = t^3 \rangle.</math><ref name="Coxeter 1940">{{cite journal |last=Coxeter |first=H.S.M. |date=1940 |title=The binary polyhedral groups and other generalizations of the quaternion group |journal=Duke Mathematical Journal |volume=7 |number=1 |pages=367–379 |url=https://projecteuclid.org/journals/duke-mathematical-journal/volume-7/issue-1/The-binary-polyhedral-groups-and-other-generalizations-of-the-quaternion/10.1215/S0012-7094-40-00722-0.short |url-access=subscription |doi=10.1215/S0012-7094-40-00722-0}} § 4 The case when ''l'', ''m'', ''n'' are positive.</ref>
Generators with these relations are given by
:<math>r = i \qquad s = \tfrac{1}{2}(1+i+j+k) \qquad t = \tfrac{1}{2}(1+i-j+k),</math>

with <math>r^2 = s^3 = t^3 = -1</math>.

There is 1 element of order 1 (element 1), one element of order 2 (<math>e_5=-1</math>), 8 elements of order 3, 6 elements of order 4 (including <math>e_3=r</math>), 8 elements of order 6 (which include <math>e_{14}=s</math> and <math>e_{18}=t</math>).

===Subgroups===
[[File:Binary tetrahedral group subgroups.png|thumb|260px|The ''binary tetrahedral group'', 2T=<3,3,2>, has 2 primary subgroups:<BR>
• [[Quaternion group]], Q=<2,2,2>, index 3<BR>
• [[Cyclic group]] Z6=<3>, index 4.]]
The [[Quaternion group#Propertie|quaternion group]] consisting of the 8 [[Lipschitz unit]]s forms a [[normal subgroup]] of 2T of [[index (group theory)|index]] 3. This group and the center {±1} are the only nontrivial normal subgroups.

All other subgroups of 2T are [[cyclic group]]s generated by the various elements, with orders 3, 4, and 6.<ref>SL<sub>2</sub>('''F'''<sub>3</sub>) on [http://groupnames.org/index.html#?SL(2,3) GroupNames]</ref>

==Higher dimensions==
Just as the tetrahedral group generalizes to the rotational symmetry group of the ''n''-[[simplex]] (as a subgroup of SO(''n'')), there is a corresponding higher binary group which is a 2-fold cover, coming from the cover Spin(''n'')&nbsp;→&nbsp;SO(''n'').

The rotational symmetry group of the ''n''-simplex can be considered as the [[alternating group]] on ''n''&nbsp;+&nbsp;1 points, A<sub>''n''+1</sub>, and the corresponding binary group is a 2-fold [[covering groups of the alternating and symmetric groups|covering group]]. For all higher dimensions except A<sub>6</sub> and A<sub>7</sub> (corresponding to the 5-dimensional and 6-dimensional simplexes), this binary group is the [[universal perfect central extension|covering group]] (maximal cover) and is [[superperfect group|superperfect]], but for dimensional 5 and 6 there is an additional exceptional 3-fold cover, and the binary groups are not superperfect.

==Usage in theoretical physics==
The binary tetrahedral group was used in the context of [[Yang–Mills theory]] in 1956 by [[Chen Ning Yang]] and others.<ref>{{cite journal
 | last1 = Case | first1 = E.M.
 | last2 = Karplus | first2 = Robert
 | last3 = Yang |first3 = C.N.
 | title = Strange Particles and the Conservation of Isotopic Spin
 | journal = Physical Review 
 | volume = 101
 | issue = 2
 | pages = 874–876
 | year = 1956
 | doi = 10.1103/PhysRev.101.874
 | bibcode = 1956PhRv..101..874C| s2cid = 122544023
 | url = https://escholarship.org/uc/item/2475r3j7
}}</ref>
It was first used in flavor physics model building by [[Paul Frampton]] and Thomas Kephart in 1994.<ref>{{cite journal
 | last1 = Frampton | first1 = Paul H.
 | last2 = Kephart | first2 = Thomas W.
 | title = Simple Nonabelian Finite Flavor Groups and Fermion Masses
 | journal = International Journal of Modern Physics
 | year = 1995
 | volume = A10
 | issue = 32
 | pages = 4689–4704 
 | arxiv=hep-ph/9409330
 | doi=10.1142/s0217751x95002187
 | bibcode=1995IJMPA..10.4689F
 | s2cid = 7620375
}}</ref>
In 2012 it was shown<ref>{{cite journal
 | last1 = Eby | first1 = David A.
 | last2= Frampton | first2 = Paul H.
 | title = Nonzero theta(13)signals nonmaximal atmospheric neutrino mixing
 | journal = Physical Review
 | year = 2012
 | volume = D86
 | issue = 11
 | pages = 117–304 
 | arxiv=1112.2675<!--hep-ph--> 
 | doi = 10.1103/physrevd.86.117304
 | bibcode = 2012PhRvD..86k7304E
 | s2cid = 118408743
}}</ref> that a relation between two neutrino mixing angles, derived<ref>{{cite journal
 | last1 = Eby | first1 = David A.
 | last2 = Paul H. Frampton | first2 = Paul H.
 | last3 = Matsuzaki | first3 = Shinya
 | title = Predictions for neutrino mixing angles in a T′ Model
 | journal = Physics Letters
 | year = 2009
 | volume = B671
 | issue = 3
 | pages = 386–390 
 | arxiv=0801.4899<!--hep-ph-->
 | doi=10.1016/j.physletb.2008.11.074
 | bibcode=2009PhLB..671..386E
 | s2cid = 119272452
}}</ref>
by using this binary tetrahedral flavor symmetry, agrees with experiment.
